paragraphs: Swamiji often pointed out that most people find it hard to grasp ideas they cannot see or touch. Whatever is solid and familiar feels real to us; whatever is abstract feels far away. To show how this works, he told a story from Bombay.

Two men, one a Hindu and the other a Jain, were deep in a long game of chess at the home of a wealthy merchant. The house stood close to the sea, and from the balcony the players could watch the water rising and falling below. Between moves, they started explaining the tides. One said the gods, while playing, hurled the water into a huge pit and then tossed it out again. The other disagreed: the gods hauled the water up to a mountaintop for their own use, and when they were finished, they poured it back down.

A young student sitting nearby burst out laughing. Didn't they know, he asked, that the moon's pull is what causes the tides? Both men turned on him, furious. Did he take them for idiots? Was the moon supposed to have ropes long enough to drag the ocean about? They would have nothing to do with such a silly idea.

Just then the merchant who owned the house walked in, and both sides asked him to settle the matter. He was an educated man and knew the student was right. But he could see there was no way to get the two players to accept it. So he quietly signalled to the student and offered them an explanation of his own.

Far out in the middle of the ocean, he told them, there is a vast mountain made of sponge. They had both seen sponge, so they knew how it works. The sponge soaks up a lot of water, and the sea goes down. Then the gods come and dance on the mountain, their weight squeezes the water out, and the sea rises again. The two chess players were delighted. This, at last, made sense to them!

The same men who had laughed at the moon accepted a dancing gods' sponge mountain without a second thought. The gods were already real to them, and they had handled sponge with their own hands. What could be more believable than the two working together on the sea?
learn: We tend to believe what fits the pictures already in our heads, not what is actually true. When an idea seems absurd to you, ask whether it is really wrong or just unfamiliar. Truth often needs a mind willing to stretch past the concrete.
